source.title: How LLMs are and are not myopic

record.tranche_reason: The post discusses different meanings of myopia and gives an argument about future-oriented computation. Its cited interpretability findings are from other work; its own informal architecture experiments report performance effects, not whether earlier-position features represent or causally steer later tokens as the claim versions specify.
record.gate_note: ROME is cited as evidence, not a result from this post. The post's own stop-gradient experiments report qualitative performance comparisons; those do not directly measure future-token representations or their causal effect on intermediate text.
record.test_reason: The post's own stop-gradient experiments remove the gradient through attention that would optimise past activations for later positions. They then compare performance with ordinary transformers. This is the same logic as the myopia-gap test of pre-caching in arXiv:2404.00859, so the results bear on V3. The evidence is weak: the authors call it informal and preliminary, and give no numbers.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that LLM pretraining is not cognitively or value myopic but is consequence-blind. They add that consequence-blindness breaks down with model-generated data, and that a myopic training goal does not guarantee myopic models. They also report informally that myopic (stop-gradient) transformers have worse scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: No original rhyme-planning or future-token probing method is applied. The post describes informal stop-gradient transformer experiments instead.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance cost of the myopic architecture increases with model scale; the effect is described as minimal at 117M parameters.
record.problems: The author describes the experiments as informal and preliminary and says quantitative results are unavailable. The post gives no model-specific results or uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: No probing of future tokens from a single hidden state.
No feature-level evidence or intervention showing which earlier-position features serve later tokens. Only aggregate performance gap; ROME is cited, not tested.
Chess is mentioned only as an argument, not tested.
Planning depth and heuristic explanations are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked this as discusses/T6. I reclassify it because the stop-gradient experiment is essentially the myopia-gap test later formalised in 2404.00859, run as an independent informal experiment. The study is weak: four models per architecture, no quantitative results, explicitly 'don't take this as strong evidence'. The ROME discussion is a cited result and correctly not a row. The record says controls 'y'; the traditional-transformer comparison does serve as a control.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyme-word representations, rhyme interventions, and changes to verse are not tested.
No single-hidden-state probe or measurement of predictability several positions ahead is reported.
The post argues that attention gradients incentivize useful computation for future positions, but does not measure pre-caching or intervene on such features and measure their effect on later tokens.
No open-weight rhyme-planning experiment or open attribution-graph or probing-tool result is reported.
Chess is used as an illustrative example, not as an experiment; multi-step reasoning and Sokoban are not tested.
No experiment tests planning depth or whether local features or heuristics explain apparent planning.

rows.subject: traditional and myopic transformers (four each; individual models not named)
rows.stage_stated: trained on the same data; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Trained transformers with stop gradients in attention layers to enforce prediction-accuracy myopia, compared with traditional transformers.
rows.measure: Performance reduction of myopic transformers relative to traditional transformers.
rows.value: The performance reduction from myopia was minimal at 117M parameters.
rows.note: Qualitative result from informal experiments; it measures performance, not pre-caching or the effect of future-token representations on intervening text.
rows.check: Should be linked to V3. The myopia performance gap measures how much pre-caching incentives contribute to performance. At 117M the gap is called 'minimal', which is only weak evidence for pre-caching.

rows.operation_detail: Trained transformers with stop gradients in attention layers to enforce prediction-accuracy myopia, compared with traditional transformers.
rows.measure: Performance reduction of myopic transformers relative to traditional transformers as model size increases.
rows.value: The performance cost increased with scale.
rows.note: The text reports a trend without model-specific values; it does not measure pre-caching or its causal effect on intermediate text.
rows.check: Should be linked to V3. The cost of blocking future-oriented gradients grows with scale up to 1.5B ('myopic transformers have worse scaling laws'). The text gives a qualitative trend only, with no per-model values.

relationships.condition: Larger GPT-2-style models trained from scratch (up to 1.5B)
relationships.reason: R2: blocking gradients that train past activations for future positions costs performance, and the cost grows with scale. Informal, no numbers.
relationships.display_finding: Blocking gradients that train past activations for future positions reduced performance, with larger penalties as models scaled up to 1.5B parameters.

relation.reason: The post reports its own controlled training comparisons bearing on V3, beyond discussing or citing the mechanism.

tranche.reason: Its own stop-gradient training comparison tests the contribution of future-position training incentives through a different method, using aggregate performance.

source_check.notes: The experiments are explicitly preliminary, with no quantitative performance results, named dataset, or feature-level analysis. Four models per architecture span the size range; hyperparameters were tuned separately using maximal update parameterization.

statements.correction: This study: four traditional and four myopic transformers spanning 117M–1.5B parameters; minimal performance reduction at 117M; increasing cost with scale; no quantitative performance results. Training-size coverage includes models above 1B.
statements.problem: The stated training-size coverage of <1B and not stated omits this study's explicitly reported models up to 1.5B. Its characterization of the evidence as informal is correct.
